writing.exampleCaption: Four traits, no hand-written code, all checked by the compiler.
writing.explanation:
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] generates the mechanical implementation for each field. It only works when every field also implements the trait, which turns a missing capability deep in a struct into a clear compile error naming the field.

A trait describes a capability. `Debug` supports development formatting with `{:?}`; `Clone` makes an explicit copy; `PartialEq` enables equality comparisons; `Default` provides a conventional initial value. `#[derive(...)]` asks the compiler to generate straightforward implementations for a struct or enum. The generated code follows the fields: if a field cannot be cloned or printed, the containing type cannot derive that capability automatically.

Derive only the traits a type needs. Cloning a large structure can be expensive and may hide a design that should borrow instead. A default value is useful when it is meaningful, but `Config::default()` is a poor substitute for required settings that must be supplied by the caller. For an enum, deriving `Default` needs one designated default variant. Generated `PartialEq` compares corresponding fields, which might be wrong for a domain concept whose identity is based only on an ID. In that case, write the behavior deliberately rather than assuming the mechanical result is right.

Try the sample with `println!("{a:?}")`, `a == b`, and `a.clone()`. Then add a field whose type lacks `Debug` and inspect the compiler error; derive or implement `Debug` for that field if printing it is appropriate. This shows how trait bounds propagate through a model. Treat a derive list as part of the public promises of a type, and keep those promises intentional.

A derived `Debug` formatter can reveal sensitive fields. Before printing a configuration or token-bearing struct in diagnostics, decide whether to implement a redacted formatter instead. Compiler-generated convenience still deserves a review of what it exposes.
writing.feedback: A derived impl is only as available as the traits of its fields.
